newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-SBC joins other Swiss banks with loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SBC joins other Swiss banks with loss.

text.p: Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) on Wednesday joined the other two Swiss banking giants by posting a 1996 loss after taking huge restructuring charges and provisions which should help future growth.

Analysts said SBC was probably best placed of the big three for recovery. But Swiss banking still faced problems with bad loans due to a flat domestic economy, although a fall in the Swiss franc's value offered hope of an upturn.
SBC, the country's third largest bank group, posted a group net loss of 1.955 billion Swiss francs ($1.3 billion) compared with a 1.053 billion franc profit in 1995.
Last September SBC forceast that restructuring measures and write-offs totalling 3.3 billion francs would push it into a loss of 1.9 billion.

All three big Swiss banks last year pushed ahead with massive writeoffs, job cuts and extra provisioning to try to tackle persistent economic weakness and a chronically depressed domestic real estate sector. All have said that operational improvements were already happening.
SBC's operating profits improved and it is confident of further progress in 1997 toward its medium-term target of an after-tax Return On Equity (ROE) of 15 percent.
The group's 1996 after-tax ROE was 10.1 percent.

SBC chief executive Marcel Ospel confirmed an earlier forecast for a 1997 net profit of 1.7 billion francs. "I said earlier today that we are on course for our goals. That means that I confirm this profit goal," he told reporters.
Operating profit was up 29 percent to 3.905 billion francs and net after-tax profit before extraordinary items was up 26 percent to 1.328 billion.
SBC's board will propose to shareholders that instead of a dividend for the 1996 financial year, it would make a capital repayment of 10 francs in nominal capital per registered share.
The biggest contribution to group profits came from SBC Private Banking, which increased net profit by nearly 19 percent to 1.063 billion francs.
The investment banking division SBC Warburg reported net profit growth of 55 percent to 820 million francs, generating an ROE of more than 16 percent.
Last month rival banking giant Union Bank of Switzerland posted a 1996 net loss of 348 million francs after a three billion franc charge to cover bad domestic loans.
Credit Suisse Group earlier this month reported a 2.59 billion franc loss after extraordinary charges of 5.4 billion for restructuring and bad loan provisions.
After recording the losses and elaborate restructuring schemes, both banks also said they were now ready for future earnings improvement.
But many analysts believe SBC has perhaps adopted the most thorough strategy to tackle Swiss banking's problems.

"I stick to my view that they (SBC) are most advanced in transforming the company into a new bank with clear, focused entities like private banking and investment banking," said Bank Julius Baer banking analyst Hans Kaufmann.

"At UBS I can say that the published result was better than expected. They also have attacked the transformation. But if I compare the three banks, our favourite is still SBC. UBS and Credit Suisse are still hold recommendations, but on the border to buy," he added.
Other analysts have said that investors may be expecting too much, too soon at Credit Suisse, whose share price has benefited from high hopes for new chief executive Lukas Muehlemann.
Kaufmann said the banks were still at risk as the economy was showing little sign of a revival and costs were still high, especially at Credit Suisse.

"The problem (of domestic credit risk) is not yet completely under control because it depends on recovery of the Swiss economy. Here I must say that thanks to the devaluation of the Swiss franc there are some hopes for 1998 and 1999," Kaufmann said.
Separately, Ospel said SBC Warburg had already booked in October any damages resulting from share transactions last year which are currently under investigation in Britain.
Earlier on Wednesday, Britain's Securities and Futures Authority confirmed that it was investigating SBC Warburg, but it would make no further comment on the case.
The investigation is into the alleged mishandling of the sale of 300 million pounds of European shares for an investment trust. ($ = 1.474 Swiss Francs)
